records.title: Brute force against authentication (ATT&CK T1110)
records.text: Many failed logins from one source in a short window, often against SSH, RDP, VPN or web login pages. Strong signals: dozens of failures per minute, many different usernames from one IP (password spraying), or a success right after a burst of failures. Typical response: block the source address at the perimeter, review the targeted accounts, force a password reset if a login succeeded, and enable MFA or lockout policies.

records.title: Use of valid accounts / suspicious sign-in (ATT&CK T1078)
records.text: A legitimate account signs in from an unusual country, impossible-travel location, new device or anonymising network shortly after normal activity elsewhere. Strong signals: MFA fatigue (many push prompts), sign-in followed by mailbox rule creation or bulk downloads. Typical response: revoke the user's active sessions, suspend the account pending verification with the owner, and reset credentials.

records.title: Command-and-control beaconing (ATT&CK T1071)
records.text: An internal host contacts the same external address at very regular intervals with small, similar-sized requests, often at night or outside business hours. Strong signals: fixed periodicity, rare destination seen by only one host, unusual user agent. Typical response: block the external address, isolate the internal host for investigation, and look for the same destination on other hosts.

records.title: Network service discovery / port scanning (ATT&CK T1046)
records.text: One source touches many ports or many hosts in a short window. Internet-wide scanning against public services is common background noise and usually low severity on its own; internal scanning from a workstation is much more concerning. Typical response: for external scanners, block if persistent or combined with exploit attempts; for internal sources, investigate the host.

records.title: Exploitation of a public-facing application (ATT&CK T1190)
records.text: Web or WAF logs show requests matching known exploit patterns against an internet-facing application, especially for vulnerabilities on the known-exploited list. Strong signals: payloads in parameters, unexpected server errors, followed by outbound connections from the server. Typical response: block the source, confirm the application is patched, and check the server for signs of compromise.

records.title: Data exfiltration over network (ATT&CK T1041)
records.text: Unusually large outbound transfers from a host or account to an external destination that it does not normally talk to, sometimes over encrypted channels or cloud storage. Strong signals: volume far above baseline, transfer outside working hours, destination recently registered. Typical response: block the destination, suspend the involved account if it is a user identity, and preserve logs for investigation.

records.title: Phishing (ATT&CK T1566)
records.text: A user receives a message with a malicious link or attachment, often impersonating a known service. Strong signals: look-alike sender domain, credential-harvesting page, user clicked and then signed in from a new location. Typical response: remove the message from mailboxes, block the sender domain or URL, and revoke sessions for any user who entered credentials.

records.title: Ransomware behaviour (ATT&CK T1486)
records.text: Rapid renaming or rewriting of many files on a host or file share, deletion of backups or shadow copies, and ransom notes appearing. This is critical severity and time-sensitive. Typical response: isolate affected hosts immediately, disable the account performing the encryption, and engage the incident response plan.

records.title: Common false positives
records.text: Frequent benign causes of alerts: vulnerability scanners run by the security team, uptime monitors, backup jobs producing large transfers, users mistyping passwords a few times, and travel that matches a known business trip. Check whether the source is on the organisation's allowlist or belongs to a known internal tool before taking action.

records.title: Response policy: human approval
records.text: Containment actions that change firewall rules or disable accounts require analyst approval. Never block private, loopback or allowlisted addresses. Prefer the least disruptive action that contains the threat, and record the reason for every change so it can be reversed.
